Fixture: 35_icc_rgb_curves_300x200_lossless.jxl (+ 35_icc_rgb_curves_300x200_lossless.icc)
300x200 RGB, mathematically lossless, RGB ICC profile with three
distinct 1024-entry tone curves -- the large-profile, multi-group case

Purpose
-------
Targets slice 4 (18181-1 E.4.5), and deliberately also the interaction
with the frame layer.

The profile is 6676 bytes: rXYZ/gXYZ/bXYZ, three *distinct* 1024-entry
16-bit curveType tables (gammas 2.2, 2.4, 2.6, so tagcode 2's shared-TRC
grouping cannot apply), a chad sf32 matrix, wtpt, desc and cprt. It is by
far the largest ICC payload in the fixture set and drives the E.4.5
command loop for thousands of bytes.

The image is 300x200, which is wider than the 256-sample group dimension,
so the frame that follows the profile is multi-section. Table A.1 puts
the ICC payload between the headers and the first frame in the same bit
stream: if its length were mis-read by even one bit, the TOC and every
section offset after it would be wrong. That is why tests/e2e_icc.rs
decodes this fixture's pixels as well as its profile.

  cjxl flags:   -d 0 -e 3 -x icc_pathname=<profile>

                tools/oracle-bin/PINNED_REVISIONS.txt)

                300x200 8-bit RGB (PPM P6):

                that tests/e2e_icc.rs can assert byte-exactness without an

Verification
------------
tools/make-icc-fixtures.sh checks two things on every run, and refuses to
write the fixture if either fails:

  * djxl --orig_icc_out returns a profile byte-identical to the one cjxl was
    given, so the reference really is what the codestream stores;
  * djxl decodes the pixels to a PNM byte-identical to the source, so the
    stream is mathematically lossless.

tests/e2e_icc.rs then asserts that JPXL's own E.4 decoder reproduces the
reference byte for byte, and repeats the comparison against a live djxl when
one is installed.

cjxl is used strictly as a BLACK BOX: it emits conformant streams for JPXL to
parse. libjxl's source is never read. If a rebuild at a different libjxl
revision changes these digests, that is the point of recording them -- do not
silently update them; note the revision change.
